title: Error-based SQL injection confirmation
summary: Use database parser errors as a signal that attacker-controlled input reaches a SQL query without safe parameter binding.
preconditions: The tester is authorized to test the target and parameter.
The application returns or logs enough database error detail to distinguish parser or type errors.
verification_method: Compare a normal request with a syntax-breaking request and a repaired request.
Confirm a database-specific error disappears when the quote or expression is balanced.
Repeat the request through a proxy to prove the same input controls the response.
known_failures: A generic error page can hide the database error while injection still exists.
WAF normalization may rewrite the payload and invalidate the comparison.
Escaped quotes can reach a string literal but still fail to alter query structure.
steps: Capture a baseline response for the selected parameter.
Send a single-quote or expression variant and record status, body, timing, and error text.
Use a database-specific probe that changes only if the SQL expression is evaluated.
Replay the request with a safe value and confirm the error signal returns to baseline.
Save both requests and responses as evidence before escalating to impact testing.

provenance.source_ref: OWASP WSTG v4.2: Testing for SQL Injection; CWE-89
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.

title: Boolean-based blind SQL injection
technique: Blind SQL injection using boolean predicates
summary: Infer query behavior from stable differences between true and false SQL predicates when query output and errors are not returned.
preconditions: The tester can issue repeated requests to the same stateful endpoint.
A response attribute changes consistently with a true predicate.
verification_method: Measure a true-condition and false-condition response using the same parameter and request shape.
Repeat each condition at least three times and confirm the response class is stable.
Vary only the boolean expression to rule out random content changes.
known_failures: Dynamic content or caching creates false differences.
The endpoint resets state between requests.
A numeric parameter may require a different boundary than a quoted string parameter.
steps: Select one stable observable such as body length, a known marker, or HTTP status.
Send a true predicate and a false predicate with identical surrounding syntax.
Compare repeated samples and calculate a conservative difference threshold.
Flip the predicates to confirm the signal follows truth value rather than payload text.
Record raw requests, response hashes, and timing for reproducibility.

provenance.source_ref: OWASP WSTG v4.2: Testing for Blind SQL Injection; CWE-89
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.

title: UNION-based SQL injection column and type discovery
summary: Determine query column count and compatible data types, then use a UNION SELECT to reflect a controlled database value.
preconditions: The tester is authorized to test the endpoint.
The query result is rendered in a response and accepts an injectable SELECT shape.
verification_method: Increment ORDER BY or NULL counts until the application response changes or errors.
Place a unique marker in candidate reflected columns and confirm the marker appears only when selected.
Use type-compatible expressions after the column count is established.
known_failures: ORDER BY rejection does not always prove UNION is unavailable.
CAST or database-specific type conversion can cause misleading errors.
The original query may wrap the injected expression in a subquery or limit result rendering.
steps: Start from a baseline response and preserve the original parameter value.
Use ORDER BY indices to estimate the number of selected columns.
Use UNION SELECT NULL placeholders and adjust the count until the query executes.
Replace placeholders one at a time with a unique marker to identify rendered columns.
Confirm the marker is generated by SQL evaluation, not reflected input, and save the proof.

provenance.source_ref: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: SQL injection UNION attacks; CWE-89
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.

title: Time-based SQL injection delay confirmation
summary: Confirm SQL evaluation by comparing response timing for a database sleep function against a no-delay control, with repeated measurements.
preconditions: The tester is authorized to consume a small amount of target time.
Requests can be repeated without destructive side effects.
Baseline latency is reasonably stable.
verification_method: Compare a delayed expression with a false branch that removes the delay.
Repeat both conditions and require a delay substantially above baseline variance.
Correlate the timing signal with database-specific syntax and safe control requests.
known_failures: Network jitter, queueing, and cold caches can imitate a delay.
A WAF or statement timeout may terminate the request before the delay completes.
Database-specific sleep syntax differs across engines.
steps: Measure at least five baseline requests to estimate latency and variance.
Send a conditional delay expression and record end-to-end timing and response status.
Send a control expression that evaluates to false and contains no delay function.
Repeat both variants and compare medians rather than relying on one sample.
Keep the delay short and stop if availability or rate limits become a concern.

provenance.source_ref: OWASP WSTG v4.2: Testing for Blind SQL Injection; CWE-89
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.

title: Operating system command injection in process arguments
summary: Test whether user input is passed to a shell or process launcher in a way that permits additional command execution.
preconditions: The tester is authorized to invoke the feature and any harm is bounded in the lab.
A target operation with an observable side effect or output exists.
verification_method: Compare a benign argument with a separator plus a harmless delay or marker command.
Confirm the marker appears only when the shell metacharacter is interpreted.
Use output, timing, or a controlled file marker as corroborating evidence.
known_failures: The application may pass arguments directly to exec without a shell.
Input validation can reject separators while leaving another metacharacter available.
Blind command execution may have no output channel.
steps: Identify a parameter that could be incorporated into a system command, such as a host, filename, or export option.
Send a baseline value and record output, timing, and status.
Try a semicolon or command-substitution probe with a harmless delay or fixed marker.
Check for both direct success and blind indicators such as a consistent delay.
Document the exact feature, parameter, and observable proof before further impact analysis.

provenance.source_ref: OWASP WSTG v4.2: Testing for Command Injection; CWE-78
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.

title: Jinja2 server-side template injection detection
summary: Use arithmetic template expressions with paired controls to determine whether user input is evaluated by a server-side template engine.
preconditions: The tester is authorized to submit template-like input.
A reflected or rendered response is observable.
verification_method: Submit the arithmetic expression and verify the rendered result is 49 rather than the literal text.
Submit a non-evaluating control such as {{7*'x'}} or a missing-variable expression.
Use two independent arithmetic expressions to distinguish evaluation from hardcoded output.
known_failures: Client-side frameworks can evaluate the same braces after the response reaches the browser.
HTML encoding can hide successful server evaluation from a visual check.
WAF rules may block braces without proving the template path is safe.
steps: Send a baseline value and preserve the exact response.
Submit {{7*7}} and inspect the raw response body, not only the rendered page.
Submit a control that should produce different output only if server-side evaluation occurs.
Correlate the input location with templates, CMS fields, email templates, or report generation.
Stop at proof of evaluation and avoid destructive object traversal unless the scope explicitly allows it.

provenance.source_ref: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Server-side template injection; CWE-1336
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.

title: Client-side template injection detection
summary: Distinguish browser-side template evaluation from ordinary text reflection by using expressions that render a unique result after JavaScript executes.
preconditions: The tester can inspect the page after JavaScript execution.
The reflected input reaches a client-side template context.
verification_method: Compare raw HTTP response with browser DOM output.
Use two different arithmetic expressions and verify the DOM changes predictably.
Inspect console or DOM mutations to confirm client-side evaluation.
known_failures: Server-side rendering can also evaluate template syntax.
Framework interpolation can be escaped in one context and evaluated in another.
A reflected literal 49 or precomputed value can cause a false positive.
steps: Capture the raw response to confirm whether the expression is already expanded.
Load the page in a controlled browser and inspect the resulting DOM.
Use a second arithmetic expression to prove evaluation rather than static reflection.
Identify whether the sink is an HTML attribute, text node, or script context.
Record the raw response, DOM state, and browser console evidence together.

provenance.source_ref: PortSwigger: XSS without HTML - Client-Side Template Injection with AngularJS; CWE-79
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.

title: XXE external entity file disclosure
summary: Test whether an XML parser resolves external entities supplied in attacker-controlled XML and returns them in parsed output.
preconditions: The tester is authorized to upload or submit XML.
The response includes parsed values or a downstream error reveals them.
verification_method: Submit a document with a harmless local entity and check whether the resolved value appears.
Compare with a document that defines an internal entity to prove entity expansion itself.
Verify that disabling external entities removes the observed output.
known_failures: Modern parsers disable external entities by default.
Out-of-band access may be possible even when file contents are not reflected.
A WAF can reject DOCTYPE while another XML parser path remains reachable.
steps: Identify an endpoint or importer that parses XML and returns parsed fields.
Send a well-formed baseline XML document and confirm normal parsing.
Add a harmless external entity pointing to a local metadata file.
Inspect the response for the resolved value or a parser error containing it.
Repeat through each XML-consuming feature because parser configurations can differ.

provenance.source_ref: OWASP WSTG v4.2: Testing for XML Injection; CWE-611
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.

title: NoSQL operator injection in JSON authentication
summary: Determine whether object-shaped user input is interpreted as query operators by a document database instead of as literal values.
preconditions: The tester is authorized to test the login or query endpoint.
The API accepts JSON, form-encoded nested fields, or equivalent object notation.
verification_method: Compare a normal invalid credential response with an operator-shaped request.
Use a never-matching and always-matching operator pair to confirm query semantics.
Check content type and request encoding to ensure the object reaches the query layer.
known_failures: The backend may coerce operator objects to strings before query execution.
Type validation may reject objects while allowing array or bracket syntax.
A generic error can conceal a successful authentication state change.
steps: Capture a baseline failed login and note cookies, tokens, status, and response timing.
Submit an object with a comparison operator that differs from an impossible value.
Attempt alternate encodings such as nested form fields when the API accepts them.
Look for authentication state changes rather than only response text.
Save the raw request and compare state before and after the probe.

provenance.source_ref: OWASP WSTG v4.2: Testing for NoSQL Injection; CWE-943
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.

title: LDAP injection in search filters
summary: Test whether untrusted input changes an LDAP search filter so that matching records differ from the intended query.
preconditions: The tester is authorized to query the directory-backed feature.
An input is combined into an LDAP filter or distinguished name.
verification_method: Compare normal, no-match, and wildcard or parenthesis probes for distinct result sets.
Use paired filters that should match different known records.
Confirm that input escaping or a restrictive base scope removes the behavior.
known_failures: The application may sanitize only one of filter or DN context.
Blind LDAP injection can expose differences only through timing or result counts.
Directory ACLs can hide matching records even when the filter changes.
steps: Identify a login, lookup, or directory search parameter that reaches LDAP.
Capture the baseline result for a known nonmatching value.
Submit a wildcard or logically true filter fragment and compare result count and content.
Try the same probe in DN-building fields such as username or group path.
Record whether the effect is authentication bypass, data disclosure, or only query alteration.

provenance.source_ref: OWASP WSTG v4.2: Testing for LDAP Injection; CWE-90
provenance.notes: Human-curated paraphrase; no exact deep URL embedded.
